screens.title: Voice VLANs: Purpose and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: A Voice VLAN is an auxiliary VLAN configured on a switchport so that an IP phone's voice traffic is separated and prioritized while a PC connected through the same phone continues to use a data VLAN. This matters because voice packets are sensitive to delay and jitter; keeping them on a dedicated VLAN makes it easier to mark and apply QoS policies. The switch typically detects the phone using CDP and instructs it which VLAN to use for voice, so the phone tags or forwards its traffic appropriately while the PC remains on the access VLAN. A concrete example: configure an access port with data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 20 so the phone's RTP streams ride in VLAN 20 where you can apply voice QoS. A common misconception is that voice VLANs require two physical links; they do not. However, misconfiguring the access and voice VLANs — swapping IDs, or failing to enable phone detection — prevents the phone from joining the voice VLAN and can degrade call quality. Key takeaway: voice VLANs simplify cabling and QoS enforcement, but verify with show interfaces switchport to confirm the phone is detected and the voice VLAN applied. How would you validate voice traffic is prioritized in your own network?

Definition

What a Voice VLAN does

Voice VLAN maps phone traffic to a dedicated VLAN to preserve QoS while the PC uses the access VLAN on the same port.

Phone detection
The switch uses CDP to detect IP phones and assigns the configured voice VLAN automatically.
Why QoS matters
Separating voice makes it straightforward to mark and prioritize RTP packets at the switch.
Common mistake
Swapping access and voice VLAN IDs or failing to enable phone detection can leave phones untagged and unprioritized.
Concrete Example
vlan 10
 name DATA
vlan 20
 name VOICE
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1

Verification
Use the command show interfaces GigabitEthernet1/0/1 switchport to confirm the voice VLAN and that the phone was detected via CDP.

Voice VLANs let you enforce QoS for phones while keeping a single physical port for both phone and PC.

screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the sequence from device connection to QoS enforcement helps prevent configuration mistakes. The typical flow starts when a phone powers up and uses CDP to announce itself to the switch. The switch recognizes the phone and, if configured, tells it which VLAN to use for voice. screens.title: Private VLANs (PVLANs) — Concept and use cases
screens.narratorSegment: Private VLANs provide a way to restrict communication between hosts that share the same subnet and primary VLAN. This is valuable in environments like shared hosting, DMZs, or multi-tenant racks where you want each tenant or server to reach the shared gateway but not each other. PVLANs divide a primary VLAN into secondary VLANs classified as isolated or community. Isolated secondary VLANs prevent all direct host-to-host communication except to promiscuous ports, which typically connect to a router or firewall. Community secondary VLANs allow communication among hosts in that community and with promiscuous ports, but not with other communities or isolated VLANs. Configuring PVLANs requires mapping the secondary VLANs to a primary VLAN and assigning switch ports as promiscuous, isolated, or community. A typical mistake is forgetting the private-vlan association step, which yields hosts that cannot reach the gateway or that can talk unexpectedly to others. Key takeaway: PVLANs let you enforce intra-subnet security policies without creating separate subnets, but plan the mapping and port roles carefully and verify connectivity. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Private VLANs
Concept

Primary and secondary VLANs

A primary VLAN contains secondary isolated and community VLANs that enforce who can talk to whom while remaining in the same IP subnet.

Isolated
No direct host-to-host communication; only promiscuous ports are reachable.
Community
Hosts within the same community can communicate and also reach promiscuous ports.
Use cases
  • Shared hosting where tenants must reach a gateway but not each other.
  • DMZs to prevent lateral movement between servers while allowing firewall access.
  • Multi-tenant racks to maintain single-subnet addressing and isolation.
Common mistake
If you forget to associate secondary VLANs with the primary, hosts may lose gateway reachability or isolation will not apply as expected.

screens.title: PVLAN mapping and port roles
screens.narratorSegment: PVLAN architecture is best understood by mapping the relationships between the primary VLAN, secondary VLANs, and port roles. The primary VLAN is the container; you then configure secondary VLANs as isolated, community, or promiscuous. A promiscuous port is typically the gateway — it can talk to all secondary VLANs. Isolated ports can only communicate with promiscuous ports, making them ideal for hosts you want fully isolated from peers. Community ports can communicate with peers in the same community and with the promiscuous port. For example, create primary VLAN 100 and then secondary isolated VLANs 101 and 102 and community VLAN 103. Map them with private-vlan association 101,102,103 under VLAN 100. Then set the gateway interface as promiscuous and host ports with host-association pairs mapping the primary to the correct secondary. A frequent source of trouble is incorrect host-association values or forgetting the private-vlan association, which can produce unreachable hosts or unexpected connectivity. Takeaway: document your PVLAN mapping and verify with show vlan private-vlan after configuration. PVLAN mapping and port roles means map secondary vlans to a primary and assign port roles explicitly; promiscuous ports are gateways, isolated ports never peer.. screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the different PVLAN port roles prevents incorrect assumptions about reachability. Promiscuous ports are the most permissive: they can communicate with all ports in the PVLAN domain, and are typically where routers or firewalls connect for gateway services. Isolated ports are the most restrictive: they cannot communicate with any other isolated or community ports — their only allowed path is to promiscuous ports. Use isolated ports when preventing lateral movement between hosts is required. Community ports are mid-level: members of the same community can talk to each other and to promiscuous ports, but not to isolated ports or other communities. A common mistake is assigning a host to the wrong secondary VLAN or misconfiguring the host-association pair. Takeaway: choose the port role intentionally based on whether hosts need peer-to-peer connectivity or only gateway access. screens.title: VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP): modes and risks
screens.narratorSegment: VTP is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that distributes VLAN configuration across switches in the same domain. It operates in Server, Client, and Transparent modes. Servers can create, modify, and delete VLANs and advertise those changes. Clients receive and apply those updates but cannot originate VLAN changes. Transparent mode forwards VTP advertisements but does not apply them to its local VLAN database; transparent switches can have locally configured VLANs not advertised to the domain. A critical operational risk is the VTP revision number: a single switch configured as a server with a higher revision can overwrite the VLAN database across the domain, deleting VLANs and causing outages. That is why a common best practice is to set new or unknown switches to Transparent mode until you verify their VTP domain and revision number, or to avoid VTP entirely in favor of manual configuration or orchestration. A misconception is thinking VTP always simplifies life; it can simplify configuration but also makes a single mistake propagate widely. Takeaway: treat VTP with caution, control server access, and verify revision numbers before connecting new switches. screens.title: Safe VTP deployment workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When adding a switch to a VTP domain, follow a safe workflow to avoid unintentionally replacing the VLAN database. First, inspect the switch's current VTP domain and configuration revision. If the revision number on the new switch is higher than the domain, it can overwrite active VLANs when the device is set to server mode. Start by setting new switches to Transparent mode so they do not apply VTP updates. Next, verify the VTP domain name and password if one is used. If you must use VTP Server mode, clear or set the revision to zero on the new switch before enabling server mode and confirm the domain name matches. In many enterprise practices, new switches are kept in Transparent mode until an administrator intentionally synchronizes VLANs. A misconception is that enabling VTP server on a new switch is harmless; it is not. Takeaway: always verify revision numbers and domain alignment, prefer Transparent for unknown devices, and keep tighter administrative control over VTP servers. screens.title: Trunking and native VLAN configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Trunking allows multiple VLANs to traverse a single physical link by tagging frames. The industry standard is 802.1Q, which inserts a four-byte tag to identify VLAN IDs except for the native VLAN, which sends untagged frames. Configure trunk encapsulation explicitly where required using switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q, then set switchport mode trunk. In this lesson you will build a practical mental model of advanced VLAN and trunking features used in enterprise switching. Next you will learn VTP modes and the risks of uncontrolled VLAN propagation, and finally we cover trunk encapsulation and native VLAN security. Each topic includes concrete configuration examples and common misconfiguration traps you will want to avoid in production. By the end you will be able to configure a switch port for voice and data, design a PVLAN domain with isolated and community ports plus a promiscuous gateway, and follow safe VTP and trunking practices. Think about a campus closet with IP phones and guest hosts — the techniques here let you keep voice quality, secure tenant isolation, and consistent VLAN state across switches without accidental outages. Second, you'll describe Private VLANs to create isolated and community groups inside a single primary VLAN, a common pattern for shared hosting or DMZ segments where hosts must reach a gateway but not each other. Third, you'll analyze VTP modes — Server, Client, Transparent — and how changes propagate, including the risk of a higher revision overwriting a domain. Finally, you'll identify common misconfigurations in advanced VLAN and trunking setups and apply troubleshooting steps. Each objective ties to hands-on verification: show commands, private-vlan mapping checks, and testing reachability to validate your changes and avoid outages.

You will run verification commands like show vlan brief, show vlan private-vlan, and show interfaces switchport to confirm mappings and port modes. A Voice VLAN is an auxiliary VLAN configured on a switchport so that an IP phone's voice traffic is separated and prioritized while a PC connected through the same phone continues to use a data VLAN. This matters because voice packets are sensitive to delay and jitter; keeping them on a dedicated VLAN makes it easier to mark and apply QoS policies. The switch typically detects the phone using CDP and instructs it which VLAN to use for voice, so the phone tags or forwards its traffic appropriately while the PC remains on the access VLAN. A concrete example: configure an access port with data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 20 so the phone's RTP streams ride in VLAN 20 where you can apply voice QoS. A common misconception is that voice VLANs require two physical links; they do not. However, misconfiguring the access and voice VLANs — swapping IDs, or failing to enable phone detection — prevents the phone from joining the voice VLAN and can degrade call quality. Key takeaway: voice VLANs simplify cabling and QoS enforcement, but verify with show interfaces switchport to confirm the phone is detected and the voice VLAN applied. Private VLANs provide a way to restrict communication between hosts that share the same subnet and primary VLAN. This is valuable in environments like shared hosting, DMZs, or multi-tenant racks where you want each tenant or server to reach the shared gateway but not each other. PVLANs divide a primary VLAN into secondary VLANs classified as isolated or community. Isolated secondary VLANs prevent all direct host-to-host communication except to promiscuous ports, which typically connect to a router or firewall. Community secondary VLANs allow communication among hosts in that community and with promiscuous ports, but not with other communities or isolated VLANs. Configuring PVLANs requires mapping the secondary VLANs to a primary VLAN and assigning switch ports as promiscuous, isolated, or community. A typical mistake is forgetting the private-vlan association step, which yields hosts that cannot reach the gateway or that can talk unexpectedly to others. Key takeaway: PVLANs let you enforce intra-subnet security policies without creating separate subnets, but plan the mapping and port roles carefully and verify connectivity. Understanding the different PVLAN port roles prevents incorrect assumptions about reachability. Promiscuous ports are the most permissive: they can communicate with all ports in the PVLAN domain, and are typically where routers or firewalls connect for gateway services. Isolated ports are the most restrictive: they cannot communicate with any other isolated or community ports — their only allowed path is to promiscuous ports. Use isolated ports when preventing lateral movement between hosts is required. Community ports are mid-level: members of the same community can talk to each other and to promiscuous ports, but not to isolated ports or other communities. A practical example: two VMs in the same community VLAN can exchange traffic directly, while two VMs in separate isolated VLANs cannot reach each other but both reach the firewall on the promiscuous port. VTP is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that distributes VLAN configuration across switches in the same domain. It operates in Server, Client, and Transparent modes. Servers can create, modify, and delete VLANs and advertise those changes. Clients receive and apply those updates but cannot originate VLAN changes. Transparent mode forwards VTP advertisements but does not apply them to its local VLAN database; transparent switches can have locally configured VLANs not advertised to the domain. A critical operational risk is the VTP revision number: a single switch configured as a server with a higher revision can overwrite the VLAN database across the domain, deleting VLANs and causing outages. That is why a common best practice is to set new or unknown switches to Transparent mode until you verify their VTP domain and revision number, or to avoid VTP entirely in favor of manual configuration or orchestration. A misconception is thinking VTP always simplifies life; it can simplify configuration but also makes a single mistake propagate widely. Takeaway: treat VTP with caution, control server access, and verify revision numbers before connecting new switches.
